atoms.text: Synthetic companions as consumer products: humans can buy partners designed to be compatible, so love becomes a pre-tested product category.
The compatibility test: a scientist develops a test that predicts whether a relationship will last, so intimacy is converted into a score.
The woman who is secretly manufactured: the protagonist discovers her own synthetic origin, so her memories and desires become design decisions.
Programmed love versus chosen love: if a partner was designed to fit you, the feeling is real but the freedom behind it is questionable.
The designer and the designed: a creator falls for the synthetic partner he helped make, so authorship and desire entangle.
Synths with a service life: synthetic bodies degrade on a schedule, so romance is shadowed by planned obsolescence.
The failed test: a couple takes the compatibility test and scores badly, so a number threatens to override their felt connection.
The synthetic ex-partner: a machine grieves a human relationship, so heartbreak is shown to be a learned capacity.
The authenticity of manufactured feeling: the story asks whether an emotion is less real if it was engineered, so the audience must choose a criterion.
The design lab as dating market: researchers prototype companions in a corporate setting, so intimacy is industrialized.
The reveal of the maker: the protagonist learns who built her, so origin becomes a rival for love.
Two kinds of love: one partner offers safety and compatibility, the other offers uncertainty, so the story stages a choice between designed and spontaneous attachment.
The right to be unhappy: a perfect partner may be a prison, so the film asks whether conflict is necessary for love.
The memory that predates the body: implanted memories give the synthetic person a past she never lived, so nostalgia is a manufactured resource.
The slow reveal: the synthetic origin is disclosed late, so the audience's earlier sympathy is retroactively re-read.
Love as maintenance: relationships require ongoing repair, so the story treats romance as labor rather than magic.
